sources.title: Tragedy and Hope: A History of the World in Our Time
sources.author: Carroll Quigley
sources.description: A wide-ranging historical synthesis of financial capitalism, imperial administration, international diplomacy, world wars and the Cold War. This supplied PDF is a retyped, annotated edition rather than a facsimile of the 1966 printing. Accounts distinguish Quigley’s interpretations from the later introduction and visible editorial insertions.
sources.pageConvention: All citations use 1-based pages of this 1,090-page PDF. These are not page numbers in the original Macmillan printing. January 1 and the first of a month are plotting anchors for dates whose day is not given.
sources.coverage: Selective, substantive extraction across the book’s institutional and political chapters, with emphasis on finance, empire and connections through the 1950s; selected 1960s developments extend the chronology. This is not an exhaustive index of every name, battle or theoretical passage. Selected institutional, financial and imperial passages in chapters 5–14 (PDF pages 47–229), with particular attention to banking mechanisms, Rhodes–Milner affiliations, constitutional reforms and the diplomatic origins of the First World War. Civilizational theory and passing references are not exhaustively indexed. Additional selected pages158–186 address foreign customs supervision, Japan’s political-economic organization and Chinese republican instability. Substantial reading of PDF pages 230–307, 399–417, and 449–454 within chapters 15–38, concentrating on the Versailles settlement, collective security, reparations, central-bank cooperation, stabilization and the 1931 crisis, British political institutions and labor, and the New Deal. This is a selective event-and-network digest, not an exhaustive transcription of every country chapter. PDF pages 472–792, chapters 39–65: Japanese and Italian aggression, British appeasement and institutional networks, European war, Allied strategy and postwar institutions, atomic diplomacy, and Cold War formation through 1950. The supplied PDF contains bracketed editorial interpolations; this digest does not attribute those additions to Quigley. Dates retain the precision supported by the supplied text, and known internal date inconsistencies are identified rather than silently repaired. Substantive reading of PDF pages 793–994, covering nuclear strategy, Korea, Eisenhower institutions, Soviet succession, Iran, Suez, Cuba, and Asian/African decolonization; selected late-book analysis pp 1011,1031–1034 and concluding 1963–1964 developments pp 1088–1090. Summaries exclude recognizable bracketed editorial interpolations. Citations use PDF page numbers, not printed-page labels.

Quigley describes Kennedy accepting CIA assurances before the Bay of Pigs invasion, then managing the 1962 missile crisis as a direct Soviet-American confrontation. In the late-book social analysis, the author also places Kennedy within an informal Atlantic Establishment through support for Britain and connections with the British Embassy and the Ormsby-Gore family; this is an interpretation of influence, not formal membership.

Scott’s note 80 cites Larry Kolb’s account of a 1950s friendship between John Kennedy and Khashoggi, reportedly corroborated by Khashoggi. The account remains a secondary personal claim; the separate Kennedy-assassination book titles in notes do not themselves establish affiliations.

milestones.name: British national branches merge with international-affairs institutes
milestones.description: Quigley says that by1939 the IPR branches in the United Kingdom and three British dominions had merged with their local institutes of international affairs.
details: The cited passage distinguishes local branch mergers from the continuing international IPR association. It says that the two kinds of institutes already had closely overlapping officers before the mergers.
The American IPR did not merge with the Council on Foreign Relations. This milestone is therefore a partial institutional transformation, not a universal merger or dissolution of the IPR.

milestones.name: Senate inquiry scrutinizes IPR
milestones.description: Quigley describes the McCarran subcommittee’s1951 inquiry seeking to connect American policy toward China with the Institute of Pacific Relations.

relationships.description: Quigley describes Naguib’s public role, premiership and presidency before Nasser displaced him.

relationships.label: Nationalizes the company
relationships.description: Quigley dates Nasser’s nationalization of the canal company to July 26,1956, following the Aswan financing crisis.

relationships.label: Trains and commands the force
relationships.description: Quigley identifies Glubb’s long-standing British command of Jordan’s Arab Legion and discusses his 1956 dismissal.

relationships.label: Monarchy sustained by the army
relationships.description: Quigley treats the Legion and external financial support as critical to Hussein’s position; the connection is institutional support rather than an invented officer rank.

relationships.label: Egyptian leader in the union
relationships.description: The book connects Nasser’s political influence with the Egyptian-Syrian union and its eventual breakdown.

relationships.label: Emergency peacekeeping force
relationships.description: Quigley describes the UN force sent to supervise the post-Suez evacuation of Egyptian territory and Gaza.

relationships.label: Secretary-general
relationships.description: Quigley describes Hammarskjöld’s mission helping end the 1958 troop deployments in Lebanon and Jordan.

relationships.label: Land reform conflicts with company holdings
relationships.description: This is an adversarial policy connection, not company membership: Quigley discusses redistribution of unused United Fruit acreage and the resulting confrontation.

relationships.label: Supported exile assault in 1954
relationships.description: Quigley attributes training, financing, equipment and operational direction to the CIA in Castillo Armas’s assault.

relationships.label: Obtains declaration against Guatemala
relationships.description: Quigley describes Dulles’s pressure at the Caracas OAS meeting as a diplomatic precursor to the intervention.

relationships.label: Revolutionary leader
relationships.description: Quigley traces the movement’s name to the failed 1953 revolt and distinguishes its initial reformist supporters from the later Communist administrative apparatus.

relationships.label: Trade negotiations in February 1960
relationships.description: The relationship records the visit and sugar-for-supplies agreement described by Quigley, not a claim that the two held the same organizational office.

relationships.label: Party leadership enables consolidation
relationships.description: Quigley argues that control of appointments and party hierarchy was decisive in Khrushchev’s rise and defeat of the 1957 challenge.

relationships.label: Leader before 1953 succession struggle
relationships.description: The account distinguishes Stalin’s control of party, state, army and policing hierarchies before his death.

relationships.label: Early successor and Khrushchev rival
relationships.description: Quigley describes Malenkov briefly holding the secretaryship and premiership, then participating in the attempt to remove Khrushchev.

relationships.label: Senior Stalinist and leadership rival
relationships.description: Quigley describes Molotov’s opposition to Khrushchev’s relaxation and his eventual exclusion for anti-party activity.

relationships.label: Diplomatic partner later displaced as premier
relationships.description: The book follows their joint state visits and cooperation before Khrushchev absorbed Bulganin’s premiership.

relationships.label: Military support followed by removal
relationships.description: Quigley places Zhukov’s army resources behind Khrushchev’s survival in the 1957 challenge, then describes his removal from office later that year.

relationships.label: Belgrade reconciliation recognizes national paths
relationships.description: Quigley links the 1955 reconciliation with recognition of different national routes to socialism and with subsequent satellite instability.

relationships.label: Declares Hungary’s withdrawal
relationships.description: The book describes Nagy’sNovember 1,1956 neutrality declaration and appeal to the UN; the relationship records attempted withdrawal, not lasting removal from Soviet military control.

relationships.label: Leader associated with the Great Leap Forward
relationships.description: Quigley discusses Mao’s resource strategy, nuclear requests and large-scale reorganization of rural society.

relationships.label: Founder and leader
relationships.description: Quigley identifies Nkrumah’s founding of the party and its 1951 electoral victory while he remained imprisoned.

relationships.label: Studies in London
relationships.description: Quigley names the London School of Economics as part of Nkrumah’s educational path before his return to Accra.

relationships.label: Pan-African organizing partnership
relationships.description: Quigley credits Padmore with organizing an independent-African-states initiative for Nkrumah.

relationships.label: Promotes Ghana-Guinea-Mali union
relationships.description: The book presents Nkrumah’s Pan-African hopes through the Ghana-Guinea association and later inclusion of Mali.

relationships.label: Guinean participant
relationships.description: Quigley follows Guinea’s rejection of the French Community into its association with Ghana and Mali.

relationships.label: Organizes the French-centered grouping
relationships.description: The source places Houphouët-Boigny behind the late 1960 move toward the Brazzaville Twelve.

relationships.label: Atlantic elite connection in Quigley’s interpretation
relationships.description: Quigley argues that Kennedy’s support for Britain in 1938–1940 opened English and then American Establishment connections. This is the author’s analysis of an informal elite, not a formally enrolled membership.

relationships.label: British diplomatic and family connection
relationships.description: Quigley cites Kennedy-family connections with the British Embassy and Harlech as an illustration of an Atlantic network.

relationships.label: Son of William Ormsby-Gore
relationships.description: The ambassador and fifth Baron Harlech is distinct from the older William Ormsby-Gore in the Anglo-American Establishment records; Quigley explicitly identifies the father-son relationship.

relationships.label: Older political association
relationships.description: Quigley identifies Harlech’s father as an old associate of Milner when discussing Kennedy’s Atlantic connections.

relationships.label: Older political association
relationships.description: The passage names Leo Amery alongside Milner in explaining the earlier generation of the British-American Establishment.

relationships.label: Preferred presidential candidate in 1952
relationships.description: Quigley describes older Wall Street, university and foundation circles preferring Eisenhower over Taft, distinguishing this from the outlook of Republican rank-and-file voters.

relationships.label: Control attributed to Morgan interests
relationships.description: Quigley describes AT&T as controlled by Morgan in his comparison of corporate assets in 1930. Morgan here identifies the financial interests and institutional network, not a claim that the elder J. P. Morgan was alive in 1930.
relationships.evidence: Control relationship asserted by Quigley; not independently verified

relationships.label: Control attributed to Morgan interests
relationships.description: Quigley identifies United States Steel as Morgan-controlled when discussing billion-dollar corporations in 1909.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Commercial subsidiary and merger partner
relationships.description: Quigley calls Guaranty Trust Morgan’s principal commercial-bank subsidiary, includes it in a wider banking nexus, and describes the April 24, 1959 merger as ending Morgan’s separate existence. His later account characterizes this as absorption into the banking subsidiary.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Founder of predecessor partnership
relationships.description: Quigley traces the firm to George Peabody and Company, founded in London in 1838. This is a predecessor relationship, not a claim that Peabody founded the later incorporated entity.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: FBI official receiving Borden letter
relationships.description: Quigley identifies Hoover with the FBI as the recipient of Borden’s accusation against Oppenheimer; the passage does not show that Hoover originated or proved it.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Submitted accusation letter
relationships.description: Quigley dates Borden’s letter to Hoover to November 7, 1953 and criticizes its allegations as a biased recycling of old material.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Accusation criticized by Quigley
relationships.description: Quigley reports Borden’s accusation of probable Soviet agency while explicitly criticizing the accusation. This link records the attack, not evidence of espionage.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Laboratory head
relationships.description: Quigley identifies Oppenheimer as head of Los Alamos and describes Groves appointing him despite known derogatory information. The two passages differ in the appointment year, so no exact date is asserted here.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Thermonuclear design suggestion
relationships.description: Quigley credits Ulam with a February 1951 suggestion to Teller that led to the successful thermonuclear design.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Trustee under Rhodes’s final will
relationships.description: Quigley says Rosebery became a trustee under Rhodes’s last will after the Uganda negotiations.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Joined Rhodes’s secret group
relationships.description: Quigley says Rosebery replaced his father-in-law Rothschild in Rhodes’s secret group; this is the author’s account of an informal circle.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Imperialist within Liberal Party
relationships.description: Quigley identifies Rosebery as a Liberal imperialist opposed to the party’s Little Englander wing.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Conditional financial contribution
relationships.description: Quigley says Rhodes contributed money in return for a promise that the party would not abandon Egypt; the passage supplies no amount for this contribution.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Continued use of Milner’s administrators
relationships.description: Quigley says Selborne took over and continued to use the Kindergarten after succeeding Milner in 1905.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Actual founder in Quigley’s account
relationships.description: Quigley calls Curtis the actual founder of Chatham House while distinguishing him from its financial supporters.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Astor family ownership
relationships.description: Quigley attributes ownership of The Times since 1922 to the Astor family. The person link represents Waldorf’s family interests, not sole individual ownership.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Astor family financial support
relationships.description: Quigley names the Astor family among Chatham House’s chief financial supporters; this does not specify Waldorf alone as the donor.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Control and influence asserted by Quigley
relationships.description: Quigley attributes domination and later control of The Times to the Rhodes–Milner group, with an exception for 1919–1922. This is his analytical claim about influence.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Financial support
relationships.description: Quigley names the Rhodes Trust and Abe Bailey as suppliers of money to the journal.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Editor
relationships.description: Quigley identifies Lothian, Philip Kerr, as the journal’s editor.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Interlocking national institutes
relationships.description: Quigley describes British-dominion IPR units as interlocking with international-affairs institutes and later calls national institutes autonomous branches. This does not make the worldwide IPR a single subsidiary of Chatham House.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Constitution writer and council officer
relationships.description: Quigley says Greene wrote the 1926 constitution, channelled funds, and held American Council treasurer and chair posts and International Council chairmanship.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Early establishment participant
relationships.description: Quigley identifies Greene as an early figure in establishing the Council on Foreign Relations after the Paris Peace Conference.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Secretary at Paris Peace Conference
relationships.description: Quigley says Greene served as secretary to the Reparations Commission in 1919.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Resident and contact with Round Table
relationships.description: Quigley says Greene lived at Toynbee Hall while stationed in London in 1918 and met the Round Table group through that residence.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Assistance securing professorship
relationships.description: Quigley says Greene wrote to Curtis after losing his investment-banking job and obtained a two-year international-relations professorship at Aberystwyth.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Covenant drafter
relationships.description: Quigley credits Hurst with wording critical Covenant articles. This is a drafting role, not evidence of employment in the Secretariat.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Semi-autonomous attached organization

relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Semi-autonomous attached organization

relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Secretary and vice-president predecessor

relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Joint nomination and career support

relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Central-bank policy cooperation

relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Secretary of state

relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: British foreign secretary

relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Prime minister after Labour victory

relationships.label: French premier

relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: President of Fifth Republic

relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Dispute over command and consultation
relationships.description: Quigley describes De Gaulle’s rejected proposal for a tripartite directorate and limits on French participation in integrated command. The passage does not say France left the alliance.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Participation and command disputes
relationships.description: Quigley describes France’s NATO commitments and disputes about the Mediterranean fleet, nuclear basing and integrated air defense in 1958–1959.
relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Overthrow operation attributed to CIA

relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.label: Coup and struggle for authority

relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.

relationships.evidence: Attributed to the supplied Tragedy and Hope body text; not independently verified.
